claims.claim: Style should suit the story; a wrong style is comic for ten pages, and the narrator's voice is inseparable from style.
claims.quote: the style should suit the story

claims.feature: narrator may comment; author may not
claims.claim: First person puts the reader inside the story and lets the narrator comment on actions, whereas authorial comment is usually ruinously bad.
Narrators are either openly unreliable or pretend to be totally reliable, but all are unreliable because people write books and people cannot be trusted.
claims.quote: narrators that pretend to be totally reliable

claims.feature: reader sees self in the text
claims.claim: Off-the-wall interpretations no longer surprise him because readers look into the story and see themselves.
claims.quote: what they are seeing is themselves

claims.claim: Fictional villains have narrow viewpoints; a real villain never thinks he is a villain, which shapes how bad men narrate themselves.
claims.quote: a real villain never thinks he's a villain

claims.claim: Characterization is done only by showing the character thinking, speaking and acting characteristically, never by telling the reader about him.
claims.quote: You simply show it and shut up.

claims.claim: Do not start a story without an ending in mind; the ending may change but there must always be a destination.
claims.quote: you should always have a destination

claims.claim: He does almost no research before writing and fills in world details as he reaches them, researching as he goes (what Greeks ate for breakfast: nothing).
claims.quote: I do research while I'm writing the book.

claims.claim: In 'The Tree Is My Hat' the ex-wife's name Mary Christmas is never stated; the reader finds it out by deduction.
Severian began as a costume (boots, trousers, no shirt, cloak, mask, sword) from which Wolfe deduced the man, an executioner.
Wolfe says the storytelling contest in the third New Sun volume is strictly padding added when the publisher split the book.
claims.quote: a storytelling contest that's strictly padding

claims.claim: Wolfe attributes the shorter paragraphs and looser tone of his later books to criticism for being unreadable and overcomplex, after which he decided to loosen up.
claims.quote: criticism for being unreadable and overcomplex

claims.feature: difficulty as duty to the reader
claims.claim: He sets himself hard technical challenges with narrators because an author who makes everything easy for himself bores the reader.

claims.feature: ghost who does not know he is dead
claims.claim: Weer's unreliability is that he is a ghost, and ghosts often do not realize they are dead.
claims.quote: Ghosts often don't realize they're dead.

claims.feature: narrator talking himself into a false identity
claims.claim: Marsch in Fifth Head knows he is not a real Earthman but is trying to talk himself into believing he is.
claims.quote: trying to talk himself into believing that he is

verdicts.trueWording: "Other than that, the style should suit the story."
verdicts.note: Clarkesworld 2008 fetched raw (curl, browser UA, HTTP 200). Quote verbatim. All limbs on page: 'Imagine The Wings of the Dove as told by Huck Finn. It would be funny for ten pages, but . . .' and 'the author's voice, or the narrator's, it's so closely linked to style that I see no point in discussing it separately.'

verdicts.trueWording: "If the author comments from his viewpoint, it's usually ruinously bad."
verdicts.note: Clarkesworld 2015 raw (HTTP 200). Quote verbatim. Page: 'When you have a first person narrator, you are much more into the story. Also, the first person narrator can comment from his viewpoint on actions.' Note the page's 'you are much more into the story' is the writer's vantage as much as the reader's; the claim's 'puts the reader inside the story' is a mild gloss but consistent with the answer's contrast to third person distance.

verdicts.trueWording: "they are always unreliable because people are writing books and people can't be trusted"
verdicts.note: Clarkesworld 2015 raw. Quote verbatim within: 'There are narrators that are openly unreliable and there are narrators that pretend to be totally reliable. But they are always unreliable because people are writing books and people can't be trusted, you know?' Every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: "I've been doing this too long to be surprised"
verdicts.note: Clarkesworld 2015 raw. Quote 'what they are seeing is themselves' is verbatim ('Somebody can look into the story and what they are seeing is themselves'), and the non-surprise is on the page. But the page attributes the non-surprise to long experience, not to readers seeing themselves; the two remarks sit side by side without the causal link the claim asserts.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the causal 'because' — the page gives long experience, not readers seeing themselves, as the reason he is no longer surprised

verdicts.trueWording: "a real villain never thinks he's a villain"; fictional villains "have very narrow viewpoints"
verdicts.note: Clarkesworld 2015 raw. Quote verbatim and the two villain limbs are on the page verbatim in substance. The third limb is an added gloss: the answer is about villains' viewpoints and the human condition, and says nothing about narration or how bad men narrate themselves (the word 'narrat-' appears only in the separate unreliable-narrator answer).
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'which shapes how bad men narrate themselves' — the page makes no claim about narration in the villain answer

verdicts.trueWording: "You do not characterize by telling the reader about the character... You simply show it and shut up."
verdicts.note: Black Gate 2010 raw (HTTP 200). Item 4 of Wolfe's numbered advice list: 'You do not characterize by telling the reader about the character. You do it by showing the character thinking, speaking and acting in a characteristic way. You simply show it and shut up.' Every limb verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: "Do not start a story unless you have an ending in mind."
verdicts.note: Black Gate 2010 raw. Item 5: 'Do not start a story unless you have an ending in mind. You can change the story's ending if you wish, but you should always have a destination.' Quote verbatim; both limbs (ending may change; always a destination) on page.

verdicts.trueWording: "how much research I do before I start writing. The answer is, almost none."
verdicts.note: Black Gate 2010 raw. Quote verbatim. Page continues: 'If it's a book on Ancient Greece, what is it about Ancient Greece that I need to know? What did Ancient Greeks eat for breakfast?' and, asked, 'They didn't eat breakfast!' — supporting research-as-you-go and the breakfast parenthesis.

verdicts.trueWording: "the ex-wife... is named Mary Christmas. I never say that - you find out by deduction"
verdicts.note: Black Gate 2010 raw. Quote verbatim; the page spells the title 'The Tree is My Hat' (lower-case 'is'), a typographic difference only. All limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: black boots, trousers, no shirt, black cloak, mask, big sword — "He's an executioner."
verdicts.note: Black Gate 2010 raw. Quote verbatim, and the costume-first origin is fully on the page: the costuming panel, then 'Black boots... Black trousers... No shirt. Black cloak... A mask. A big sword. And I thought - who is this guy? The answer was obvious. He's an executioner.' But the page never names the character: 'Severian' occurs zero times in the interview (grep count 0); Wolfe names only 'the Urth of the New Sun series'. The identification is the verifier's inference, not the source's word.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the name 'Severian' — the page names only the New Sun series, never the character

verdicts.trueWording: "If you look in the third book, you will find a storytelling contest that's strictly padding."
verdicts.note: Black Gate 2010 raw. Quote verbatim. The split limb is supported immediately before: 'My publisher thought that I should divide it into two books and build each book up... That's what I did.'

verdicts.trueWording: "criticism for being unreadable and overcomplex... 'Well, I'll loosen up.'"
verdicts.note: MIT Technology Review 2014 raw (HTTP 200, full article text retrieved, section 'EDITING AND WRITING'). Quote verbatim inside: 'It's that I've gotten so much criticism for being unreadable and overcomplex and hard to get into and all this stuff. And I thought, "Well, I'll loosen up."' The shorter-paragraphs/looser-tone description is the interviewer's, which Wolfe re-explains ('It's not that, really') by the criticism — exactly the attribution the claim makes.

verdicts.trueWording: "If you make everything easy for yourself as an author, you bore the reader."
verdicts.note: MIT Technology Review 2014 raw, section 'UNRELIABLE NARRATORS AND CRAFT'. Interviewer: 'With your narrators, you set yourself difficult technical challenges.' Wolfe's answer is the quoted line. Both limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: "He's a ghost. Ghosts often don't realize they're dead."
verdicts.note: MIT Technology Review 2014 raw, same section. Quote verbatim (typographic apostrophes normalized). The interviewer names Weer as 'unreliable in this particular sense: he's dead, and doesn't know it', and Wolfe affirms 'He's a ghost.'

verdicts.trueWording: "He knows he's not a real Earthman, but he's trying to talk himself into believing that he is."
verdicts.note: MIT Technology Review 2014 raw, same section, answering whether John Marsch understands he is really V.R.T. Quote verbatim; every limb on the page.
